newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS to issue audited report on Nazi gold dealings.
newsitem.headline: BIS to issue audited report on Nazi gold dealings.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) will lift a veil of secrecy over its past on Monday by releasing a report about its trade with Nazi gold to try to dispel lingering suspicions of wrongdoing.

The report does not reveal any new findings about BIS's dealings with Germany's Reichsbank during World War Two, banking sources said. But is significant because it is based on BIS archives, up to now hermetically sealed to public scrutiny.

The release of the report, which has been audited by a leading accounting firm, will provide a foretaste of BIS's archives before their expected opening, BIS general manager Andrew Crockett told the Swiss newspaper Tribune de Geneva on Tuesday.

BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, has been preparing to open its archives to historians for the last two years and informed sources expect BIS's board, which is made up of the Group of 10 (G10) central bank governors, to approve opening up the vaults next year.

BIS management has already said that its archives are open to the Volcker Commission and the commision of historians that has been charged by the Swiss government to look into the country's dealings with Nazi Germany.

The decision to publish the report shows BIS's eagerness to be open and honest about its past dealings with Nazi Germany, which have come under new scrutiny as part of the debate of the fate of Jewish accounts in Swiss banks.

BIS's dealings with Nazi Germany were criticised during and after World War Two. But any defence of its actions lacked credibility because BIS's archives were sealed and it could neither prove nor disprove any allegations.
Part of the mystique that surrounds BIS is its secrecy and unique status of being beyond Swiss banking laws.
BIS's charter protects its assets in time of peace or war from expropriation or confiscation and the import or export of gold or currency can neither be prohibited nor restricted.
The report is based on a detailed account that was sent to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato last year.
D'Amato has spearheaded U.S. inquiries into dormant Jewish accounts in Switzerland and been a vocal critic of Swiss banks' handling of the sensitive issue.

A U.S. government report, prepared under the direction of Under Secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, is expected to be released shortly and be very harsh on the Swiss role as bankers and even money-launderers for the Third Reich.

BIS, which is owned by central banks and does not conduct business with private persons, had dealings with Nazi gold because of its role as an overseer of German reparations to the Allied governments after World War One.
Under the Young Plan and the Hague Agreement, which established the BIS in 1930, BIS invested money in Germany and in return the Reichsbank paid interest to BIS.
Between 1939 and 1945 the Reichsbank physically deposited 12 tonnes of gold at BIS'S account with the Swiss National Bank (SNB) in Berne, half of which was interest payments.
The other half covered German debts in a European postal clearing system and payments to Yugoslav railways.
Until 1943 the Reichsbank mainly paid interest in currency, but after 1943 all interest was in the form of gold.

A total of 13.5 tonnes of gold was actually transferred by the Reichsbank to BIS'S accounts, but a final shipment of 1.5 tonnes in April 1945 never reached Switzerland because it was stopped at the German-Swiss border.
After World War Two, BIS handed back 3.7 tonnes of gold to the Allied Powers. The gold was identified as looted by the Germans from the central banks of the Netherlands and Belgium.
